en: The Fourth Pāda. (Topic 1:
[The lifelong repetition]). (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.1): The lifelong repetition is a property of the ritual action, because of the context.

In the injunction, “One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] for as long as one lives,” there is a prescription of a time-period sufficient for one’s lifetime specifically regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual performed for the sake of a desired end, such as heaven.
Nor is there a contradiction with the specific times such as the full moon (paurṇamāsī);
for both are compatible through a relationship of pervader and pervaded, just as in the case of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the afternoon.

For this very reason, since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā*) [to prefer one over the other], even when two points of time are prescribed, there is a prescription for two distinct ritual performances (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, by the force of the prescription of a duration sufficient for life, the performance of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices recurs at every full moon and so forth.

Thus, it might be argued that the fruit such as heaven is obtained from a single comprehensive performance (*vyāpaka-eka-prayoga*) which encompasses the various partial performances (*vyāpya-prayoga*) [occurring throughout life]. To this we reply: this is not a prescription of time, because it would result in the fault of [the word *darśapūrṇamāsa*] being used as an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of time.

Therefore, since the connection of living with the action is understood through the *ṇamul* suffix prescribed under the heading of "connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusaṃbandha*), and since it is not logically tenable for the principal act to be repeated merely to conform to a subordinate time— which would require assuming a relationship such as being delimited by its own duration— it follows that even the meaning of the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) would have to be treated as something to be enjoined.
Consequently, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the relationship perceived is simply that of being a condition (*nimitta*).

For in that case, since the recurrence of the prompted act (*naimittika*) for every individual occasion (*pratinimitta*) is obtained through logical necessity, the verbal meaning is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Furthermore, being an occasion (*nimittatva*) consists in the state of having a mandatory performance that conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its own [occurrence].

For example, in the case of an eclipse of Rāhu, the state of having a mandatory performance that conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of the eclipse belongs to that ritual bathing (*snāna*).

And here, the purport of the injunction lies precisely in its conformity with the negative concomitance (vyatireka). Consequently, because the injunction makes known the necessary performance of the occasional rite when the occasion is present, the sin incurred by non-performance is inferred.

Furthermore, regarding the performance, as in the case of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice, the fruit in the context of obligatory and occasional rites is the incidental destruction of sin, based on supplementary scriptural statements such as, "By [this] dharma, one removes evil."

However, where the cause—such as the *rathantara-sāman*—is present, the effect can be obtained through the very recitation [of the rule] itself; thus, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by that other means of knowledge, the purport of the injunction lies solely in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For this very reason, in the absence of the *rathantara*, there is an absence of the precedence of the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgratva*).

And therefore, since the status of "living" as a causal condition (*nimitta*) is understood from the term *yāvajjīva* in accordance with considerations of parsimony (*lāghava*) and so forth, it is established that, in deference to that, this is indeed a distinct application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of destroying sin. // 1 //
Thus ends the first section concerning the fact that [the observance] lasts as long as one lives.

(B2) [An exposition establishing that the Vārttikakāras agree that there is an inquiry into whether the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites is distinct or non-distinct when conjoined with the quality of being lifelong.

Having prescribed the optional performance in the statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the author cites the passage recorded in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa: "As long as one lives... and so forth.

The statement "one performs the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives" is an illustration that includes other similar sentences as well. Although the author of the *Bhāṣya* has here undertaken an inquiry into whether [the lifelong performance] is a property of the ritual (*karmadharma*) or a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*) in accordance with the *Sūtra*, this is improper; for since the inquiry is connected to the third chapter, it would result in a lack of topical consistency within the section defining "difference" (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), which has not yet been concluded. Furthermore, [he asks]: "Is there a difference in the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites when they are conjoined with the qualification of 'as long as one lives'?"

Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* maintained that this very same ritual performance (*prayoga*) intended for specific desires (*kāmya*) is itself limited by the duration of one's entire life (*yāvajjīva*), thereby establishing the distinction or non-distinction of the performance based on its conformity to such characteristics;

[this was done] because he was dissatisfied with the conclusion established in the aforementioned *Vārttika*, and thus determined that the meaning of the section consists precisely in the distinction or non-distinction of the application (*viniyoga*).

However, in reality, even though the time "as long as one lives" is an auxiliary element of the performance, it cannot—like the evening and morning times—act as a differentiator of the performance within the previous performance, since there is no possibility of obstruction when that [previous] performance is already occupied by the evening and morning times.

Likewise, although the *nimitta* (occasioning condition) is impossible in the prior performance (*pūrvaprayoga*), it is not a constituent part of that performance. Even though the established performance occurring at specific times such as the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) may lead to another application (*viniyogāntara*) of the ritual action, it does not lead to a different performance (*prayogāntara*). Therefore, because it does not differentiate the performance like time and other factors do, there is no possibility of an inquiry into whether the performance is differentiated or undifferentiated; or even if such an inquiry were somehow possible, it would fall under the same discussion as the *aveṣṭi-adhikaraṇa*.

Since it is not appropriate to investigate [the matter] here due to the lack of relevance of such an investigation, and being dissatisfied with the statement of the Vārttikakāra, [the author] states in the Kaustubha the connection with the definition— namely, that because the cause (*nimitta*) is connected with the application (*viniyoga*), the distinction or non-distinction of the application prompted by it was previously unmentioned anywhere, and thus constitutes the subject matter (*pādārtha*) of this section— and likewise, that although the cause is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) and thus a differentiator, it does not entail [the status of] being something not to be taken up (*anupādeya*), because the nature of the cause itself is not something to be taken up.

Since the investigation into whether there is a difference in application (*viniyoga*) and the incidental connection (*prāsaṅgikī-anantara-saṅgati*) are clear, the author does not state the doubt mentioned by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), but instead states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself: "It is indeed for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*)."
(The presentation of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] that this is an injunction of an accessory [guṇavidhi] within the optional (kāmya) Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual:

By stating "the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual" [in the phrase *darśapūrṇamāsakarmaṇi*], the author aims to dispel the misconception—suggested by the writing in the Vārttika that "this very same performance (prayoga), which is optional, is itself delimited by the duration of one's life"—that this is an injunction regarding time for the optional performance.

(By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only the optional" [*kāmya eva*], the author indicates that in the final position [siddhānta] there is no support from the context [prakaraṇa], whereas in the prima facie view there is such support.)

Furthermore, because the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) lacks the necessary qualities for application in this sentence, it is not accepted even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Moreover, since there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) to rely on that [injunction] when enjoining the time such as the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the same consequence would follow here as well. Therefore, the meaning is that when the time is enjoined with reference to the ritual action (*karman*) itself, it occurs according to the method to be explained;
however, it is not an injunction of time by way of restating the performance.

In the Siddhānta, although there is an acceptance of the context known as *adhikāra* (qualification) through the establishment of a further application of this very rite by way of its connection with a specific motive (*nimitta*), the particle "only" (*eva*) is employed in the phrase "only in the case of the optional [rite]" (*kāmya eva*) to indicate that, while the former context is accepted, the context characterized by the expectancy of "how" (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) is not accepted in the Pūrvapakṣa, whereas it is accepted in the Siddhānta.
(The determination that the word *yāvajjīvam* ends in the suffix *ṇamul*, not as a cause [for a grammatical operation], but as a prescription of time:
"It is a prescription of time."

The meaning is that even though the word *yāvajjīvam* ends in a *ṇamul* suffix, its reference to time is established through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), just as in the expression "it remains as long as the body exists.

Furthermore, since even a form ending in *ṇamul*—such as in the case of *abhikrāmam juhoti* ("he offers while stepping forward")—is seen to have the sense of a causal condition (*nimitta*), it is appropriate here for this to be an injunction regarding time alone.
The phrase "like the afternoon and so forth" [refers to this].

The meaning is that just as in the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* injunction, although two [acts] are prescribed for the time of the afternoon of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), there is no contradiction due to their being of a single time because one [act] serves as the delimiting factor for the other; so too here [in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*], it is appropriate. (In this prima facie view, the objection raised by the ancients regarding the necessity of indicating repetition through the verbal root *yaji* is refuted.

Here, the ancients [hold that] in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since it is impossible to accommodate a duration of time sufficient for a lifetime by performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices only on the full moon and new moon days, the verbal root *yaji* must indicate repetition (*abhyāsa*) in order to prescribe the performance of the sacrifice repeatedly.
That which was raised as an objection in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states in order to refute it: "sufficient for livelihood" (jīvanaparyāpta).
And thus, by the use of the word "eva" (only/just), it is indicated that [the action] does not have repetition as its defining characteristic, much less its status as something to be enjoined.
The intention is that even the sūtra, "Repetition lasts as long as one lives," should be interpreted as referring to repetition in its implied sense.

(An exposition based on the position that there is a separate injunction for the application of the pervader distinct from the application of the pervaded): And thus, just as in the sentences concerning the full moon and other [parvan] days there is an injunction for the application of the pervaded characterized by time,
so too in the sentence regarding "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), the injunction of an application characterized by time is not untenable.

Therefore, since a single property is admitted to be distributed across as many pervaded applications as are sufficient for life—each being a distinct further property serving as the delimitor of the respective prescriptibility—it follows that the result arises precisely from the pervader-application distributed across those pervaded applications; thus he says: "Heaven and so forth."

The meaning is this: when there is an expectation of a fruit for an action characterized by the application of both the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), since it is enjoined specifically for the sake of heaven by the sentence "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), heaven and so forth alone are the fruit;
it is not that the destruction of sin is a separate fruit because of its being enjoined for the sake of destroying sin by the *yāvajjīva* (lifelong) injunction.
And thus, through those applications sufficient for one's lifetime, only a single fruit such as heaven is produced.
The meaning is that it does not exclude [the former].
And this formulation of another pervader (vyāpaka) based on the application of the pervaded (vyāpya) has been established according to the method stated in the Kaustubha.
(An examination of the fact that heaven and so forth occur only at the end, neither in the interim nor through the mere destruction of sins,

etc.): In reality, however, since the matter is settled by the employment of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) alone, there is no evidence whatsoever for accepting the employment of its respective pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*);

for even though the sentences concerning the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and so forth enjoin those respective times by way of restating a pervasive application, the very possibility of introducing those respective times as delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the period of life is itself the restrictive factor.
Indeed, it is not possible for the non-exclusive [period of] living to serve as a delimiter during the times of the full moon and so forth.
Therefore, this is precisely the injunction for the performance characterized by a specific time for living that has not yet been obtained.

Otherwise, since the times such as the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) could be introduced through a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*), the statement regarding the absence of contradiction would fail to withstand the charge of being redundant.

For this very reason, the explanation of the connection provided in the *Kaustubha*—which takes recourse in a distinction of application (*viniyoga-bheda*) because there is no distinction in the performance (*prayoga*) and thus no possibility of a connection with the subject matter under discussion—is logically consistent.

It should be understood that even by that much, there is no impairment to this distinction of results— namely, that the result such as heaven arises only from a performance lasting for the duration of one's life as delimited by times such as the full moon, and not from an intermediate performance, nor is the destruction of sin the result.

(An explanation of how the term *yāvat* indicates a restatement of a repetition obtained through reasoning, because it is impossible to enjoin time since the meaning of the word *yāvat* is a property of the person):

For in the expression *yāvajjīvam*, since the word *yāvat* denotes totality, its literal meaning is a property of the person; therefore, as it cannot logically be a property of the ritual action, one must necessarily resort to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the period of living within the word *jīva*. With this in mind—namely, that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there would be the fault of having to resort to an indication [of a repetition]—[the author speaks of] the occurrence of an indication of repetition.

Setting aside what was stated by the predecessors, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) while presenting the definition of time as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Because it would result in the definition of time."

Based on the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) that "suffixes [occur] when there is a connection between verbal roots" (*dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ*), since the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a root when there is a connection of the meaning of that root with the meaning of another root, and because this connection is expressed by the *ṇamul*, one might expect a specific relation to be required. However, considering that the cognition of that specific relation—in the form of being a cause—is obtained through the force of the word's intended meaning (*tātparya*) as a restrictor, there is no need for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in my view to convey it; with this intention, he says:
"From this" means:

The opponent’s intention in avoiding the charge of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is that, since the understanding of time is established through the very mode of relation (*saṃbandha-vidhi*), even for me there is no occurrence of *lakṣaṇā*; this is indicated by the phrase "and in resorting to the relation.

Furthermore, although there is no resulting syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—either because the meaning of the word *yāvat* is itself the object of injunction (*vidheya*) due to being expressed by a single word, or because it enjoins a qualified performance (*viśiṣṭa-prayoga-vidhāna*)—the charge of prolixity (*gaurava*) remains; this is indicated by the phrase "due to prolixity" (*lāghavāt*).
There is prolixity when [time] appears as a mere relation (*saṃsarga-vidhi*).

By the word "only" (eva), it is indicated that what is to be excluded is the view that both appearing as a category of object (*padārtha*) and being a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) constitute the cause [of the cognition].
Because it is obtainable through reasoning.

The meaning is that because there is a possibility of repetition based on the distinction between various lives consisting of vital functions, and because the totality pertaining to life is already established as being connected with occasional causes, this is a restatement (anuvāda).
(An exposition on the fact that here, when life is the occasion (*nimitta*), there is indeed the injunction of another application [of the act], etc.):

For this very reason—where there is an understanding of performance through the hearing of an injunctive suffix (*vidhi-śravaṇa*), there one resorts to a relationship characterized by being an occasion (*nimittatva*) in view of the occasion in its capacity as a prompter of performance (*anuṣṭhāpaka*). However, where there is such hearing by way of a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), as for example in "as long as the milking lasts" (*yāvaddohaṃ*), since there is no understanding of performance itself, there is no connection with another meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in view of that [performance] in its capacity as a prompter.
However, the distinction is that "it" (the action) consists precisely in having a time delimited by itself;
as it is stated in the Vārttika: "In this case, the mention of time is appropriate, for this is a description of the present; here there is no dependence on any external cause."
Therefore, in the case of the scriptural injunction, the time is taken as exceeding the milking;
for if here too it were enjoined that "one should sleep or sit until the milking is finished," [the same would follow].
Therefore, by what means could the status of milking as a *nimitta* (condition) be precluded?
Consequently, since living is the *nimitta*, and although a *nimitta* prompts performance, there is no evidence that it necessitates the entire ritual application (*prayoga*),
this is merely another application of these [acts]— which have their own inherent applications— by way of connection with the *nimitta*, just as in the case of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).
The fruit such as heaven does not result from the mere performance of the pervasive ritual application alone.

Furthermore, because it forms a single syntactical unit with other scriptural injunctions regarding time—such as the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*)—it is one's life, as delimited by the forenoon and the full moon day, that constitutes the occasion (*nimitta*). Consequently, neither another lunar date nor a single full moon day alone serves as the occasion for the performance.

The consequence of repetition (āvṛtti) arises either because of the difference in the occasion (nimitta) consisting of the life-span delimited by that [time], or because of the occurrence of repetition;

however, the objection that repetition would result by taking the difference in life at every moment—even within the Full Moon sacrifice (Paurṇamāsī) delimited by the forenoon—is untenable precisely because it is impossible. This is the intended meaning.

(Definition of the nature of being a cause) Furthermore, the nature of being a cause (*nimittatva*) does not consist merely in being an instigator of performance, as is the case with desire and the like;
for if it were so, such performance would already be established by the science of erotics (*kāmaśāstra*) alone, which would result in the redundancy of this statement.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the nature of the occasion (*nimitta*)—which includes the implication of its necessity for performance—is stated as follows: "And the state of being an occasion... (*nimittatvaṃ ca*).

Regarding the fact that an injunction associated with a specific occasion (*nimitta*) conveys the idea of transgression (*pratyavāya*) when it is not performed: since the necessity of performance cannot be accomplished by a person acting intentionally of their own accord,

the author says— intending to convey that an injunction associated with a specific occasion, by the force of its inherent fitness, makes known that the non-performance of the enjoined act is a cause of transgression.
"And for this reason."

Therefore, the intention is that, in accordance with such being the cause [of the result], there is the statement of an injunction regarding the performer’s duty— the rule (niyama) in the form of a necessary obligation which is established by implication— according to the sūtra: "Or rather, it is the duty of the performer, because of its connection with the Vedic text" (Jaimini 2.4.2).

(An exposition of the fact that the *viśvajit* maxim does not apply, thereby establishing that the purpose [of the injunction] is the destruction of sin as found in the supplementary portion of the text.

Here, the Prābhākaras maintain that although the injunction makes known that the non-performance of what is enjoined produces demerit (*pratyavāya*), there is no fruit whatsoever for its performance. However, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, on the other hand, has stated that since the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix is necessarily in need of an objective (*bhāvya*), even if a fruit is accepted from the performance, the preservation of the prior absence of demerit—which would otherwise arise from non-performance—constitutes the fruit.
To refute both of those [positions], he says: "And in the case of an instrument... (karaṇe ca).

Since a desired fruit such as heaven cannot be established as a necessary consequence, and because it is improper to assume heaven as the fruit according to the *Viśvajit* maxim, when there is a requirement for a specific fruit, it is determined from supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*)— such as "By dharma one dispels evil," "The Brahmin, reciting [the mantra] during the morning twilight, removes the sin of the night," and "Whatever sin I have committed by night, whatever sin I have committed by day, whether by mind, speech, or with my two hands"— that the fruit is the destruction of the demerit (*pratyavāya*) produced by the performance of prohibited acts.
This is the meaning.
Although the phrase "by means of dharma" has no further syntactic supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is indeed a complete sentence (*vākya*) in itself.

Nevertheless, because these [verses] included under the word "etc. (*ādi*) are supplementary to the previously mentioned injunctions for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), they are described as "vākyaśeṣa" (supplementary statements).

Regarding the statement that the destruction of sin is a secondary result (*anuṣaṅgika*), this refers to the fact that while one engages in the rite out of fear of the transgression incurred by non-performance, the absence of such engagement is required for the destruction of sin to occur.
The refutation of the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* should be consulted in the *Kaustubha*.

In order to avoid the consequence of [the definition] being merely a characteristic of the sign (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), he clarifies once more the very point already stated in the section concerning the *rathantara-sāman*: "But where... and so forth.
He concludes the established tenet [with the words] "ataśca" (and therefore).

(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections: Regarding the purpose, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is only a single optional (*kāmya*) performance consisting of a form practiced throughout one's life; thus, in modified rites (*vikṛti*) such as the *saurya* sacrifice, the lifelong repetition is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, even for one who does not desire a specific result, there is a single performance consisting of a form practiced at the evening and morning times, and it is completed right there.

In the interval between the morning and evening times, another [rite] is performed in the same manner; however, because there is no extension of the occasion (*nimitta*) to the solar [deity], the performance does not continue for as long as one lives. This has not been stated because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the first section concerning the fact that [the observance] has lifelong duration as its cause.
(B1) (Section 2 / [A.2 Pāda 4 Adhikaraṇa 2]) Name:
Even though there exist means of differentiation in the case of the Agnihotra and other such rites, there is no difference in the ritual action (*karma*).

For, by means of differentiating authorities (*bhedaka-pramāṇa*), one understands that one's own statement is intended for the origination of a ritual action; since it is impossible for what has already originated to originate again, the status of the action as being distinct is established. However, in the present case, even though the aforementioned authorities lead to the understanding of an intention toward origination, there is no difference in the ritual action because—due to the difference in persons—it is possible for each single action to originate everywhere with respect to those persons who study their respective recensions (*śākhā*). Indeed, all recensions are not to be studied by all persons.

In the injunction for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), just as in the case of "he chooses the Adhvaryu," the singularity and one's own ownership are intended to be significant; therefore, the study of multiple recensions (*śākhā*) is untenable.

Nor does this imply that the study of recensions belonging to other Vedas is likewise precluded; for, in accordance with other scriptural statements such as "having studied the Vedas," it is understood that the study of one recension from each of the three Vedas is what is mandatory.

For this very reason, it will be explained later that when there is a difference between Vedas, since the person is the same, the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) applies to one alone, while the mention in the other is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

But if the Veda is one, then despite the fact that every recensional branch (*śākhā*) is intent upon origination, there is no difference in the ritual action (*karma*) because of the distinction between individuals for each branch.
For this very reason, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the various auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) belonging to different branches which are contradictory in relation to a single ritual action.
And that option is not restricted according to the distinction of those respective individuals.

Since there is no evidence that those respective auxiliary elements are intended for the sake of those specific reciters, it is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice alone;
thus, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of non-contradictory auxiliaries.
Furthermore, knowledge of the auxiliary elements belonging to other recensional branches (*śākhā*) is easily obtained through the *Kalpasūtras* and similar works.

As for the statement, "Whether extensive or brief, that which is prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra," and so forth, it should be understood from the Kaustubha that this is intended as a provision for an alternative (anukalpa) when it is impossible to perform all the constituent parts (aṅgas).
Thus, the distinction between ritual acts has been established through difference of words, repetition, number, name, quality, and difference of context.
Hereafter, their application (viniyoga) will be determined. // 2 //
Thus ends the second section concerning other Vedic branches (śākhāntarādhikaraṇa).
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
The chapter is concluded.

(B2) [Examination of the Connection Following the Definition: Having completed the examination of the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—previously described according to their distinctions as origination, application, and differentiation—one now [turns] to the ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) found in the various recensions (*śākhā*) contained within a single Veda.

Although other words, names, and numbers lack the capacity to differentiate [actions], there is a thematic connection (*lakṣaṇasaṅgati*) because this section examines whether qualities (*guṇa*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), and a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*)—which do possess the capacity to differentiate—act as such differentiators. Furthermore, there is an immediate thematic connection (*ānantarasaṅgati*) by way of an exception (*apavāda*) to the differentiation of application (*viniyoga) presented in the immediately preceding section; this is clear. Thus, without stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which is of little consequence, [the author] proceeds with an illustration.
He states the established conclusion itself: "by way of the division of branches."
The phrase "contained in one Veda" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

For this very reason— according to the principle of the third book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*], namely, "by the greater number, when both are heard"— the originative injunction (*utpatti*) occurs only in that Veda where the form [of the rite] is obtained through the mention of the substance and the deity,
and not elsewhere.

In that context, since it will be established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the repetition is for the sake of a specific quality (*guṇārtha*), a doubt regarding a difference [of injunction] is untenable there; therefore, they cannot serve as examples.

Consequently, the meaning is that only those cases where a difference in originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is possible through the acquisition of form (*rūpalābha*) in both instances are to be taken as examples, because only there does a doubt regarding a difference arise.
"Even when [the conditions] exist."

(Regarding the prima facie view that even though names ending in words such as *saṃjñā* do not differentiate [actions], they may nevertheless differentiate them through qualities such as repetition and so forth:
Although the author of the Sūtras stated that names such as "the Kāṭhaka" and "the Kālāpaka" differentiate ritual actions,
in those cases, because such names refer to the texts (*grantha*), they do not refer to the rituals (*karman*).
Furthermore, because it is not mentioned by name in the Veda and because it does not pertain to the origin [of the action], its capacity to differentiate is impossible;
the justification for this in the Sūtra should be understood as being merely supplementary.

Likewise, since a different word (*śabdāntara*) also possesses the same meaning of the verbal root, its differentiation from the meaning of other roots is accepted even in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*); therefore, it is not a differentiator.
Likewise, because number serves to differentiate its own inherent substratum, it is impossible [for it to apply to another];

thus, even though other designations, words, and numbers are impossible, when there is a repetition in the form of an injunction not intended for anything else— such as the quality of being eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni— the other quality of being twelve potsherds prescribed in another scriptural passage is [excluded].

Because a quality cannot be incorporated due to its distance and lack of proximity, and because there is an absence of a commonality of qualities in what is to be adopted (*upādeya*), the plural form "among the means of differentiation" (*bhedakapramāṇeṣu*) is employed with the intention of indicating that "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) can also function as a differentiator.
He demonstrates this very point [in the following verse]: "For by the means of differentiation... (*bhedakapramāṇairhi*).

(Although the recitation (*svādhyāya*) is the objective of the injunction for study, both its being one's own and its singularity are intended to be expressed because they are included as attributes in the inferred injunction),
just as in the case of "one should choose the *adhvaryu* priest."

And by this—since the study (*adhyayana*) is the objective (*uddeśya*) with respect to the recitation (*svādhyāya*)—there might arise a doubt that the singularity inherent in the objective *svādhyāya* is not intended to be significant.

[The author responds: Just as in the case of "he chooses the *adhvaryu* priest," although the *adhvaryu* is the objective, there is an intention for the singularity because he is heard in the text as something to be taken up (*upādeya*) in the inferred injunction: "one should perform one's own duty with the *adhvaryu* who has been chosen."

Likewise, here too, in the case of an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) which is to be inferred—namely, "one should cultivate the knowledge of the meaning by means of the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) already mastered"—the fact that it is heard as something to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*) indicates the rejection of the view that its [literal] verbal form is intended (*vivakṣā*).

It is called *svādhyāya* based on the etymology "that which is studied by oneself" (*svair adhīyate*), which expresses "belongingness" (*svīyatva*) in the sense of being accepted by the person through one's own lineage of study. Thus, it is said to be "belongingness."
(An establishment of the fact that the term "svādhyāya" refers to a Vedic branch (*śākhā*) which is pervaded by the status of being a Veda.)

Because Vedic revelation (śruti) and traditional law (smṛti)— such as “One conquers the world by means of this threefold knowledge,” and “Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda in due order”—
authorize the study of the various recensions (śākhās) contained within the Vedas, the term *adhyāya* must, in accordance with that,
refer specifically to the recensions subsumed under categories such as the Ṛgveda.
And in that very context, because "one's own" (*svīya*) and "single" (*eka*) function as qualifiers,

it is intended that although the study of other branches subsumed under that [specific branch] is enjoined by means of establishing a rule for the study of a single branch— which is itself subsumed under [the category of] being an *Ṛgveda* branch and so forth, and which has been transmitted through a specific lineage of ancestors— there is nevertheless no exclusion of branches belonging to other Vedas.
He composes himself—[meaning] "he studies the Vedas."

(The demonstration that there is a difference in ritual action due to a difference in the Veda, but not a difference in the recensional branch, is as follows: because of the non-difference of the person.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no contradiction for the study of that [Veda] with respect to all persons due to the division of the Vedas, and since it is impossible to resolve the repeated hearing of injunctions contained therein by attributing them to different classes of students, both [the action and its result] would result in being established. In such a case, where there is the recitation of more extensive qualities (dharmas), the establishment [of the action] occurs there;
elsewhere, the hearing is for the sake of a subordinate quality (guṇa). Thus, the abundance of meaning will be stated as the regulating factor in the third [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

Thus, it should be understood that even in cases where there is a division of Brāhmaṇas known as the Pañcaviṃśa and Ṣaḍviṃśa within a single branch (śākhā) of the Sāmaveda, since there is no difference among the students, one [text] is an injunction (vidhi) and the other is a restatement (anuvāda), provided there is no subverting factor; however, in the absence of such [a subverting factor], they constitute distinct rites due to repetition.
This is because [the texts] are intent upon origination (utpatti).

The meaning is that there is no difference in the ritual action (karmabheda), because the repetition of the injunction is justified as making known the origin [of the rite] to those respective students who were previously unaware of it.

Thus, since the repetition of the injunction is shown to have another purpose and the argument for differentiation through mere repetition has been refuted, and since that very [repetition]— even if it implies a distinct origination (*utpatti*) due to a difference in the agent (*pramātṛ*) by way of being a "separate context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) characterized by non-presentation— does not imply a difference [in the rite] itself, [the author], intending to show that the status of being a differentiator is unestablished,
says "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) in order to refute the remaining type of difference caused by accessory qualities (*guṇa*).

Since both [texts] are equally intent upon the origination [of the rite] due to the difference in their respective reciters (*adhyetṛ*), neither possesses the status of being "taught as originated" (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) nor "taught as already established" (*utpanna-śiṣṭa*).

For this very reason, because it is impossible for one to sublate the other, when they have a single purpose, there is an option (*vikalpa*), just as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*).

Anticipating the objection that—since titles such as *Kāṭhaka* are applied to the ritual acts just as they are to the branches (*śākhā*), and since these titles could establish a restriction to specific individuals (the *adhvaryu*, etc.)—he provides the following rebuttal: [The text continues: ...because the titles such as *Kāṭhaka* apply to the ritual acts just as they do to the branches, and since through them a restriction to specific individuals—such as the *adhvaryu*—could be justified, he offers the following refutation: ... [end of fragment]
And if...

The meaning is that, since the application (*prayoga*) regarding the ritual action is based on a relationship prescribed by the texts proclaimed by Kaṭha and others, it cannot serve as a regulator for Kaṭha and the rest through a relationship of agency; therefore, the systematic restriction [of rituals] is not established by that.
[Now, the determination of the means for performing the subsidiaries belonging to other recensions:

An objection is raised: "But how can the performance of subsidiaries or principal rites belonging to other recensions be justified, given the absence of knowledge established by the injunction to study [those specific texts]? This doubt is addressed as follows:

Although the injunctions for rituals do not necessitate [the study of] their means— since knowledge regarding the subject matter of one's own branch (śākhā) and its performer is already established by the injunction to study—
that necessity is logically justified when there is an absence of such knowledge regarding the subject matter to be performed as it occurs in other branches;
this [objection] is refuted by the statement "belonging to another branch," since the performance of rites is possible through the acquisition of that knowledge via the study of Kalpasūtras.
(Refutation of the claim that the injunctions for sacrifices imply the eligibility of Śūdras):
The point is that even if such an implication were possible for a Śūdra, it is not so because of the prohibition against his studying the means [for performing them]; thus, there is a disparity.
(Resolution of the contradiction regarding the statement "much or little"):

Now, one might object that when incorporating subsidiary elements from other recensions (*śākhā*), there is the following scriptural statement: "Whether much or little has been proclaimed for anyone according to their own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, when that much of the purpose of the scripture is performed, everything is considered performed. Here, the term "one's own *Gṛhya*" (*svagṛhya*) is used as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative or figurative designation).

To dispel the doubt that there might be a contradiction because of the rule prescribing the performance of what is stated in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* or understood from one's own *Śākhā*, he says: "As for that which... and so forth.

(An Examination of the Purpose of the Prima Facie and Conclusive Positions) Regarding the purpose: according to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is neither option (*vikalpa*) nor combination (*samuccaya*) for the auxiliary elements found in other recensions; according to the conclusive position (*siddhānta*), both [apply]. This has already been stated almost entirely previously, and thus it is not repeated here.
(Conclusion of the chapter’s subject matter and summary of the subject matter of the subsequent chapter:

And regarding these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when they encounter a single object, there exists a distinction between validity and invalidity, consisting respectively in the capacity to apprehend an object not yet apprehended and the absence thereof.

Intending to show that because there is no contradiction even here, one need not investigate relative strength or weakness, [the author] concludes the subject matter of the chapter with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore), since nothing remains to be investigated.
In order to prevent the listeners from becoming indifferent and to facilitate easy comprehension, he summarizes the subject matter of the subsequent chapter with the words: "Henceforth..."

By the use of the plural "of them" (teṣām) and by the phrase "beyond this" (ataḥ param), it is indicated that the determination of the subject matter of the subsequent chapter stands in a relationship of cause and effect with the determination of the subject matter of this chapter; this connection will become clear later on.
Thus ends the second section concerning other recensions (śākhāntara).
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Prabhāvalī*, a commentary on the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, composed by Śuṃbhubhaṭṭa, disciple of Khaṇḍadeva, the ornament of poets.
Here the second chapter is completed.
